item.title: Eastern North Pacific Tropical Weather Outlook
item.description:
000
ABPZ20 KNHC 012305
TWOEP

Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
500 PM PDT Thu Oct 1 2026

For the eastern and central North Pacific east of 180 longitude:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on Tropical
Storm Nolo, located several hundred miles west of Lihue, Hawaii, and
on Hurricane Rachel, located a couple of hundred miles south of Baja
California Sur. The National Hurricane Center has issued the last
advisory on Tropical Depression Nineteen-E, located well
west-southwest of the Baja California Peninsula.

South of Southern Mexico:
An area of low pressure could form in a few days south of the
southern coast of Mexico. Thereafter, environmental conditions
appear favorable for gradual development, and a tropical depression
is likely form by the middle of next week while the system moves
slowly west-northwestward to northwestward.
* Formation chance through 48 hours...low...near 0 percent.
* Formation chance through 7 days...high...80 percent.

$$
Forecaster Cangialosi

item.description:
Issued at 200 PM MST Thu Oct 01 2026 
914 
WTPZ33 KNHC 012035

BULLETIN
Hurricane Rachel Advisory Number  19
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       EP182026
200 PM MST Thu Oct 01 2026
 
...RACHEL STRENGTHENS WHILE SLOWLY MOVING WESTWARD...
 
 
SUMMARY OF 200 PM MST...2100 UTC...INFORMATION
----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...19.4N 109.5W
ABOUT 245 MI...390 KM S OF THE SOUTHERN TIP OF BAJA CALIFORNIA
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...120 MPH...195 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...W OR 280 DEGREES AT 3 MPH...6 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...950 MB...28.06 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 200 PM MST (2100 UTC), the center of Hurricane Rachel was located
near latitude 19.4 North, longitude 109.5 West. Rachel is moving
slowly toward the west near 3 mph (6 km/h) and this slow west to
west-northwest motion is expected the next couple of days.
 
Maximum sustained winds have increased to near 120 mph (195 km/h) 
with higher gusts.  Rachel is a category 3 hurricane on the 
Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale. Additional strengthening is 
forecast the next day or so, before some gradual weakening this 
weekend.
 
Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 40 miles (65 km) from the
center and tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 150 miles
(240 km).
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 950 mb (28.06 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
SURF: Swells generated by Rachel will affect the coast of
west-central Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula through the
end of the week. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening
surf and rip current conditions. Please consult products from your
local weather office.
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 800 PM MST.
 
$$
Forecaster Kelly
item.author: nhcwebmaster@noaa.gov (NHC Webmaster)

item.title: Hurricane Rachel Forecast Discussion Number 19
item.description:
Issued at 200 PM MST Thu Oct 01 2026 
000
WTPZ43 KNHC 012036
TCDEP3
 
Hurricane Rachel Discussion Number  19
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       EP182026
200 PM MST Thu Oct 01 2026
 
Rachel's satellite presentation has improved this afternoon, with a
ragged eye becoming apparent in both visible and infrared imagery.
Deep convection surrounds the eye with cold cloud tops near -80C.
The system is situated further south than previously analyzed and
has slowed its forward speed, as anticipated. Satellite intensity
estimates have continued to climb, with subjective and objective
estimates ranging from 90 to 95 kt. Given the recent satellite
trends and eye formation, the initial intensity is raised to 105 kt
for this advisory.
 
The initial motion is west-northwestward or 290/3 kt. This slow
motion is expected to continue for the next couple of days. Then a
mid-level ridge is forecast to build to the north of Rachel, which
should induce a faster westward forward motion. Model guidance
continues to show some spread regarding exactly when this
re-acceleration will occur. The updated NHC track forecast has been
shifted slightly south to reflect the current position and is also
slower in the near term. Towards the end of the forecast period, the
track blends toward the HCCA and GDMI aids.
 
Environmental conditions remain generally favorable for further
strengthening, with warm sea surface temperatures and with the
improved structure showing a better alignment of the low- and
mid-level centers. However, models indicate some vertical wind shear
may impact the system over the next day or so, which could slow the
rate of intensification. The slow motion of the system may induce
upwelling, and this combined with the cool wake left by Polo could
inhibit strengthening. In 2 to 3 days, as Rachel begins to move
westward, it is forecast to move parallel to the 27C isotherm and
into a drier mid-level airmass, this should induce a weakening
trend. The ultimate structure of Rachel, particularly if it takes on
annular characteristics, will depend heavily on the rate of this
weakening. The NHC intensity forecast is higher than all of the
model guidance in the near term based on the current structural
trends, but then trends back toward the consensus aids later in the
period.

item.title: Remnants of Nineteen-E Forecast Discussion Number 10
item.description:
Issued at 200 PM PDT Thu Oct 01 2026 
000
WTPZ44 KNHC 012047
TCDEP4
 
Remnants Of Nineteen-E Discussion Number  10
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       EP192026
200 PM PDT Thu Oct 01 2026
 
Easterly wind shear and dry mid-level air have taken their toll on 
Nineteen-E today. Earlier microwave imagery indicated a shallow 
system that may have been open on the southern and eastern side of 
the center. More recently, nearly all of the convection has been 
sheared off, leaving only a swirl of low-level clouds. Nineteen-E is 
therefore estimated to have opened into an trough and can no longer 
be classified as a tropical cyclone. The remnants are expected to 
continue moving eastward over the next day or so before dissipating.
 
This is the last public advisory issued by the National Hurricane 
Center on this system. Additional information on this system can be 
found in High Seas Forecasts issued by the National Weather Service, 
under AWIPS header NFDHSFAT1, WMO header FZNT01 KWBC, and online at 
ocean.weather.gov/shtml/NFDHSFAT1.php
 
 
FORECAST POSITIONS AND MAX WINDS
 
INIT  01/2100Z 15.0N 123.0W   25 KT  30 MPH
 12H  02/0600Z...DISSIPATED
 
$$
Forecaster Adams
